# The provenance file on Arhat

*Catalogue entry — Arhat. Every claim below carries its chain of custody.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **अर्हत्**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (MN 10), Sāriputta Sutta (SN 47.19), Kevaṭṭa Sutta (DN 11), Etadagga Vagga (AN 1).

**2. The narrative record.** **Worthy of Gifts** — Arhat comes from √arh, "to deserve, to be worthy," with the participle -at — "the worthy one," one deserving of the alms of gods and men.  The Buddha claimed it as his own foremost title: in the canonical litany he is arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, "arahant, fully self-awakened" — a claim whose audacity the Udāna records being tested in his lifetime, when rivals demanded he prove it. **Sāriputta and Moggallāna** — The Buddha named his two greatest arahants in the Etadagga verses (AN 1): Sāriputta, foremost in great wisdom — the Dhamma's marshal, who could unfold a single line into a hundred meanings and who, questioned on his deathbed in the Sāriputta Sutta (SN 47. 19), replied only that there was nowhere he had ever clung; and Moggallāna, foremost in psychic powers, who humbled Brahmā's pride by shaking the Vejayanta palace with a toe (DN 11, Kevaṭṭa Sutta).

**3. The physical record.** The arhat's archaeology is the archaeology of the aniconic saṅgha. The Bharhut and Sanchi reliefs (2nd–1st c. BCE) show the great disciples flanking the empty throne — identifiable by label in Brahmi inscriptions: Sāriputa, Mogalāna, Maha Kāsava. The earliest anthropomorphic saṅgha images come from Gandhāra and Mathurā (1st–3rd c. CE): monks in patched robes, each with his attribute. The lohans' gallery in Chinese art is documented from the Tang — Guanxiu's sixteen (c. 891–901) survive in the Tokyo Seikado and Imperial Household collections — and the Five Hundred Lohans halls of the Song and Ming (Jingshan, Biyun, Baoguang monasteries) preserve the type at monumental scale. In Pāli lands, the arhat leaves no relic-cults of his own by design: the finished one, the tradition says, leaves nothing to enshrine but the teaching.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/arhat/](/arhat/), classified Tier 2. Tier-2 here means one preserved truth — not less important, just singular. The temple shows it and names it.

**5. The documented resonances.** **Education, Research & Knowledge**, **Mythic Name Restoration**, **Writing, Publishing & Media** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/arhat/blog/resonance/).

**6. The primary sources.** [Lotus Sutra](/texts/lotus-sutra/), [Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtras](/texts/sukhavativyuha/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**7. The continuing record.** The arhat's afterlife is the afterlife of the Theragāthā — a book of verses by the first saints, still chanted in Pāli lands, among the oldest autobiographies in the world.  Chinese temples fill halls with lohan: the Five Hundred Arhats of Beijing's Biyun Si and the sixteen of Hangzhou's Jingshan Si are national treasures; Guanxiu's originals survive in Japan, designated national treasures there too.
